claim: The mesiotemporal lobe (MTL) is implicated in memory, navigation, socio-affective processing, and higher-order perception.
source: The mesiotemporal lobe (MTL) is implicated in a diverse range of cognitive processes, notably memory, navigation, socio-affective processing, and higher-order perception (Moscovitch et al., 2005; Squire et al., 2004; Zheng et al., 2017; Milner, 2005; Eichenbaum et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2018; Eacott et al., 1994; Lee and Rudebeck, 2010; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Felix-Ortiz and Tye, 2014; Lech and Suchan, 2013).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing MTL's role in these cognitive processes.

claim: The broad role of the MTL in human cognition emerges through interactions between neural codes within the MTL and the rest of the brain.
source: Contemporary views recognise that the broad role this region plays in human cognition emerges through interactions between neural codes within the MTL and the rest of the brain (Lech and Suchan, 2013; Saksida and Bussey, 2010; Staresina and Davachi, 2009; Diana et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to contemporary research on MTL function.

claim: The MTL plays a key role in the formation of cognitive maps by providing a low dimensional representational scheme of different situational contexts.
source: Motivated by its role in spatial processing (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978), it has been suggested that the MTL plays a key role in the formation of cognitive maps (Tolman, 1948) by providing a low dimensional representational scheme of different situational contexts (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Behrens et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to theoretical work on cognitive maps and spatial processing.

claim: The broad role of the MTL in human cognition results from both its intrinsic circuitry and position within the larger cortical architecture.
source: A widely held assumption posits that the broad role of the MTL in human cognition results from both its intrinsic circuitry and position within the larger cortical architecture, which places the MTL at the apex of multiple conceptual hierarchies (Mesulam, 1998; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Chanes and Barrett, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on cortical hierarchies and MTL positioning.

claim: The mesiotemporal cortex exhibits a shift from six-layered isocortex to three-layered allocortex.
source: Unique in the mammalian brain, the mesiotemporal cortex folds in upon itself, producing the curled hippocampal formation that sits atop the parahippocampal region. This infolding is accompanied by a shift from six-layered isocortex to three-layered allocortex (Insausti et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical research on MTL structure.

claim: During ontogeny, allocortical hippocampus lacks clear lamination prenatally and exhibits a more even distribution of neurons across depths compared to isocortex.
source: During ontogeny, isocortex (from iso- 'equal') differs from allocortical (from allo- 'other') hippocampus, which lacks clear lamination prenatally and exhibits a more even distribution of neurons across depths (Sanides, 1962; Vogt and Vogt, 1919).
evidence: Supported by citations to developmental neuroscience research.

claim: Variations in cytoarchitecture are thought to be involved in the transformation from unimodal to amodal information.
source: Such variations in cytoarchitecture are thought to be involved in the transformation from unimodal to amodal information (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000), as well as degree of synaptic plasticity low in iso-, and high in allocortex (García-Cabezas et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on information processing and synaptic plasticity.

claim: The transition from allo-to-isocortex occurs in smooth streams of gradation emanating from the hippocampus.
source: The transition from allo-to-isocortex occurs in smooth streams of gradation emanating from the hippocampus (Sanides, 1962; Duvernoy et al., 2013; Braak and Braak, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The wave of laminar differentiation is phylogenetically conserved.
source: This wave of laminar differentiation is phylogenetically conserved (Sanides, 1962; Dart, 1934; Abbie, 1938; Abbie, 1942)
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative anatomy research.

claim: Classic histological studies suggested that the wave of laminar differentiation is accompanied by step-wise changes in neuronal density at various cortical depths.
source: classic histological studies suggested that the wave is accompanied by step-wise changes in neuronal density at various cortical depths (Sanides, 1969).
evidence: Supported by citation to histological research.

claim: The human MTL has exaggerated folding compared to other mammals.
source: Nevertheless, compared to other mammals, the human MTL has exaggerated folding, more extensive lamination of the entorhinal cortex as well as a more prominent appearance of the Cornu Ammonis (CA) 2 subfield, highlighting the need to characterise the region's microstructure in our species (Insausti et al., 2017; Duvernoy et al., 2013; Insausti and Amaral, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: The human MTL has more extensive lamination of the entorhinal cortex compared to other mammals.
source: Nevertheless, compared to other mammals, the human MTL has exaggerated folding, more extensive lamination of the entorhinal cortex as well as a more prominent appearance of the Cornu Ammonis (CA) 2 subfield, highlighting the need to characterise the region's microstructure in our species (Insausti et al., 2017; Duvernoy et al., 2013; Insausti and Amaral, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: The human MTL has a more prominent appearance of the CA2 subfield compared to other mammals.
source: Nevertheless, compared to other mammals, the human MTL has exaggerated folding, more extensive lamination of the entorhinal cortex as well as a more prominent appearance of the Cornu Ammonis (CA) 2 subfield, highlighting the need to characterise the region's microstructure in our species (Insausti et al., 2017; Duvernoy et al., 2013; Insausti and Amaral, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to comparative anatomical studies.

claim: Degree of laminar differentiation is generally thought to reflect the origin and termination patterns of axonal projections.
source: Degree of laminar differentiation is generally thought to reflect the origin and termination patterns of axonal projections (Barbas, 1986)
evidence: Supported by citation to research on cortical connectivity principles.

claim: Feedforward projections flow from iso-to-allocortex, whereas feedback projections flow from allo-to-isocortex.
source: Accordingly, feedforward projections flow from iso-to-allocortex, whereas feedback projections flow from allo-to-isocortex (Barbas, 1986; Hilgetag and Grant, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on directional connectivity patterns.

claim: Cytoarchitectural similarity is tightly coupled with likelihood of interareal connectivity, a principle known as the 'structural model'.
source: Furthermore, cytoarchitectural similarity is tightly coupled with likelihood of interareal connectivity, a principle known as the 'structural model' (Barbas, 1986; Beul et al., 2015; Beul et al., 2017; García-Cabezas et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to research on structure-connectivity relationships.

claim: Key fibre pathways in the MTL (perforant pathway, mossy fibres, and Schaffer collaterals) are typically defined by their relation to hippocampal subfields that are sequentially organised along the iso-to-allocortical axis.
source: Consistent with this view, key fibre pathways in the MTL, notably the perforant pathway, mossy fibres, and Schaffer collaterals, are typically defined by their relation to hippocampal subfields (subiculum, CA1-4, dentate gyrus) that are sequentially organised along the iso-to-allocortical axis (Amaral and Witter, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical research on MTL pathways.

claim: Neurobiological and functional properties of the MTL system are organised with respect to an anterior-posterior axis.
source: In addition to the iso-to-allocortical shifts that follow hippocampal infolding, neurobiological and functional properties of the MTL system also appear to be organised with respect to a second, anterior-posterior axis (Amaral and Witter, 1989; Strange et al., 2014; Witter et al., 2006; Poppenk et al., 2013; Vogel et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on MTL organization.

claim: Tract-tracing studies in rodents have shown that anterior-posterior gradients determine hippocampal connectivity to entorhinal cortices.
source: Tract-tracing studies in rodents have shown that anterior-posterior gradients determine hippocampal connectivity to entorhinal cortices (Witter et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by citation to tract-tracing research.

claim: Functional neuroimaging studies in humans have illustrated distinct combinations of anterior-posterior and lateral-medial topographies in the entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex.
source: functional neuroimaging studies in humans have illustrated distinct combinations of anterior-posterior and lateral-medial topographies in the entorhinal and parahippocampal cortex (Navarro Schröder et al., 2015; Maass et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to neuroimaging research.

claim: Data-driven analyses of resting state functional MRI have confirmed marked differentiation of anterior and posterior aspects of the hippocampus in terms of intrinsic functional connectivity.
source: Recently, data-driven analyses of resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) have confirmed marked differentiation of anterior and posterior aspects of the hippocampus in terms of intrinsic functional connectivity (Zhong et al., 2019; Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Przeździk et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent fMRI studies.

claim: The MTL is a hub of multiple large-scale networks.
source: Given the established role of the MTL as a hub of multiple large-scale networks (Smallwood et al., 2016; Vincent et al., 2006; Ojemann et al., 1997; Braga and Buckner, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to network connectivity research.

claim: Operations implemented by the internal hippocampal circuitry include pattern separation and completion.
source: This architecture could allow operations implemented by the internal hippocampal circuitry, such as pattern separation and completion (Rolls, 2016; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014; Staresina et al., 2016; Nakazawa et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to research on hippocampal computational functions.

claim: Whole-brain functional organisation can be understood as discrete communities such as the sensory, attention, and transmodal networks.
source: Contemporary neuroscience has established that whole-brain functional organisation can be understood as discrete communities such as the sensory, attention, and transmodal networks (Yeo et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to network parcellation research.

claim: The relationships between functional communities can be represented by gradients of cortex-wide connectivity.
source: and that the relationships between these communities can be represented by gradients of cortex-wide connectivity (Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to gradient mapping research.

claim: One functional gradient differentiates sensory from transmodal systems that harbour cognitive processes increasingly reliant on information from memory.
source: One functional gradient differentiates sensory from transmodal systems that harbour cognitive processes increasingly reliant on information from memory (Murphy et al., 2018; Murphy et al., 2019; Sormaz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to functional gradient research.

claim: A second large-scale functional gradient reflects the dominance of networks involved in complex tasks in which there is no predetermined schema with which to guide behaviour, also referred to as the multi demand system.
source: A second large-scale functional gradient reflects the dominance of networks involved in complex tasks in which there is no predetermined schema with which to guide behaviour, also referred to as the multi demand system (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Duncan, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to research on multiple-demand systems.

claim: Anterior hippocampus preferentially connects to transmodal isocortex and posterior hippocampus to sensory isocortex.
source: Extensive research on preferential connectivity of anterior hippocampus to transmodal isocortex and posterior hippocampus to sensory isocortex shows that the MTL architecture can reflect a large-scale functional motif (Strange et al., 2014; Maass et al., 2015; Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Przeździk et al., 2019; Libby et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to connectivity research.

claim: The study leveraged an ultra-high-resolution 3D reconstruction of a histologically stained and sliced human brain (BigBrain) to build a continuous model of the MTL architecture.
source: We leveraged an ultra-high-resolution 3D reconstruction of a histologically stained and sliced human brain (﻿BigBrain [Amunts et al., 2013]) to build a continuous model of the MTL architecture.
evidence: Describes the primary data source used in the study.

claim: The principle gradient of cytoarchitectural differentiation in the MTL, accounting for 15.6% of variance, closely approximates the geometric iso-to-allocortical axis (r = 0.76, p<0.001).
source: Unsupervised manifold learning of microstructure profile data revealed that the principle gradient of cytoarchitectural differentiation, accounting for 15.6% of variance, closely approximates the geometric iso-to-allocortical axis (r = 0.76, p<0.001; Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of histological data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The relationship between the principle eigenvector and the iso-to-allocortical axis appeared nonlinear (adjusted R2 for polynomials 1–3 = 0.58/0.59/0.65).
source: This relationship appeared nonlinear (adjusted R2 for polynomials 1–3 = 0.58/0.59/0.65)
evidence: Supported by polynomial regression analysis of the data.

claim: CA2 expressed a different cytoarchitecture than expected by its position on the geometric map.
source: and CA2 expressed a different cytoarchitecture than expected by its position on the geometric map (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lower eigenvectors were not spatially correlated with the iso-to-allocortical axis (0.01<|r| < 0.31).
source: Lower eigenvectors were not spatially correlated with the iso-to-allocortical axis (0.01<|r| < 0.31)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of eigenvectors.

claim: Microstructure profile features provided a highly accurate mapping of the iso-to-allocortical axis based on random forest regression (R2 = 0.91 ± 0.005).
source: Microstructure profile features provided a highly accurate mapping of the iso-to-allocortical axis based on random forest regression (R2 = 0.91 ± 0.005; Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by machine learning analysis shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Profile skewness, staining intensity at upper (~13% depth) and mid (~53% depth) surfaces were key features in learning the iso-to-allocortical axis (average reduction in variance: 53/41/16%).
source: Profile skewness, as well as staining intensity at upper (~13% depth) and mid (~53% depth) surfaces were key features in learning the axis (average reduction in variance: 53/41/16%; Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by feature importance analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Three key features (skewness and intensities at ~13% and ~53% depth) alone accounted for most variance in out-of-sample data (R2 = 0.86 ± 0.006).
source: These three features alone accounted for most variance in out-of-sample data (R2 = 0.86 ± 0.006; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by cross-validation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Microstructure profile skewness increased from iso-to-allocortex, which pertained to a shift from a profile with mid-depth peak to a flatter microstructure profile.
source: Microstructure profile skewness increased from iso-to-allocortex, which pertained to a shift from a profile with mid-depth peak to a flatter microstructure profile (Figure 1H, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for exemplar microstructure profiles and feature values).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intensity at ~13% depth exhibited a rapid uptick at the iso-allocortical intersection.
source: Intensity at ~13% depth approximately corresponds to the layer1/2 boundary in the isocortex and exhibited a rapid uptick at the iso-allocortical intersection.
evidence: Supported by analysis of depth-wise intensity patterns.

claim: Intensity at ~53% depth reached a minimum around the intersection of the iso- and allo-cortex.
source: Intensity at ~53% depth approximately aligns with the peak intensity of the average microstructure profile, signifying high cellular density, and reached a minimum around the intersection of the iso- and allo-cortex.
evidence: Supported by analysis of depth-wise intensity patterns.

claim: Microstructure profile skewness consistently increased along iso-to-allocortical axis regardless of anterior-posterior axis (mean ± SD adjusted R2 = 0.64 ± 0.17).
source: Independently inspecting 1 mm coronal slices of the post mortem data, we found that microstructure profile skewness consistently increased along iso-to-allocortical axis, regardless of anterior-posterior axis (mean ± SD adjusted R2 = 0.64 ± 0.17, Figure 1I left).
evidence: Supported by analysis across coronal slices shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Depth-dependent intensities were more variable along the anterior-posterior axis (13% depth: goodness of fit = 0.20 ± 0.12; 53% depth: goodness of fit = 0.40 ± 0.24).
source: On the other hand, depth-dependent intensities were more variable along the anterior-posterior axis (13% depth: goodness of fit = 0.20 ± 0.12; 53% depth: goodness of fit = 0.40 ± 0.24)
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of depth-wise intensities across anterior-posterior axis.

claim: The dynamic model showed dense, bidirectional effective connectivity across the MTL.
source: This model showed dense, bidirectional effective connectivity across the MTL (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by dynamic causal modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Deviation from the iso-to-allocortical axis was related to lower effective connectivity in both directions (to isocortex riso = −0.43, p=0.02; to allocortex: rallo = −0.44, p=0.02).
source: Deviation from the iso-to-allocortical axis was related to lower effective connectivity in both directions (to isocortex riso = −0.43, p=0.02; to allocortex: rallo = −0.44, p=0.02; difference in coefficients: z = −4.33, p=0.99, Figure 2B right).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of effective connectivity shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The final bin, containing CA4, inhibited other regions.
source: Furthermore, the final bin, containing CA4, inhibited other regions
evidence: Supported by effective connectivity analysis.

claim: The sixth bin, corresponding to the subiculum, was the strongest driver of excitatory effective connectivity.
source: and the sixth bin, corresponding to the subiculum, was the strongest driver of excitatory effective connectivity (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for subfield overlap).
evidence: Supported by effective connectivity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Effective connectivity estimates from models within thirds of the anterior-posterior axis were moderately correlated with effective connectivity estimates from the full mesiotemporal confluence model (r = 0.60/0.38/0.45).
source: Effective connectivity estimates, calculated from a model within thirds of the anterior-posterior axis were moderately correlated with effective connectivity estimates from the full mesiotemporal confluence model (r = 0.60/0.38/0.45, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The inverse correlation between deviation from the iso-to-allocortical axis and effective connectivity was not consistently observed in spatially restricted models (difference in coefficients: anterior z = −2.92, p=0.99; middle z = −1.01, p=0.84; posterior z = −0.47, p=0.68).
source: Unlike the full mesiotemporal confluence, however, we did not consistently observe inverse correlation between deviation from the iso-to-allocortical axis and effective connectivity in these spatially restricted models (difference in coefficients: anterior z = −2.92, p=0.99; middle z = −1.01, p=0.84; posterior z = −0.47, p=0.68, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of models shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Lateral dorsal attention and fronto-parietal networks exhibited stronger rs-fMRI connectivity towards the isocortical anchor of the cortical confluence.
source: Specifically, lateral dorsal attention and fronto-parietal networks exhibited stronger rs-fMRI connectivity towards the isocortical anchor of the cortical confluence, whereas posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal regions of the default-mode network and medial occipital areas in the visual network showed stronger connectivity towards the allocortical anchor (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by rs-fMRI connectivity analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal regions of the default-mode network and medial occipital areas in the visual network showed stronger connectivity towards the allocortical anchor.
source: Specifically, lateral dorsal attention and fronto-parietal networks exhibited stronger rs-fMRI connectivity towards the isocortical anchor of the cortical confluence, whereas posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal regions of the default-mode network and medial occipital areas in the visual network showed stronger connectivity towards the allocortical anchor (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by rs-fMRI connectivity analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Position on the iso-to-allocortical axis showed a parametric relation with rs-fMRI along the third functional gradient (r = −0.74, pspin <0.001).
source: A similar pattern was summarized by observing a parametric relation between position on the iso-to-allocortical axis and rs-fMRI along the third functional gradient (r = −0.74, pspin <0.001)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with spin permutation testing.

claim: The third functional gradient depicts a differentiation of the multiple-demand system.
source: which depicts a differentiation of the multiple-demand system (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Duncan, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to research on multiple-demand systems and interpretation of gradient.

claim: The association between iso-to-allocortical axis and functional connectivity appears to be specific to the third functional gradient, with higher correlation coefficients than the first (z = 12.30 p<0.0001) and second functional gradients (z = 21.33 p<0.0001).
source: The association appears to be specific to the third functional gradient, supported by higher correlation coefficients than the first (z = 12.30 p<0.0001) and second functional gradients (z = 21.33 p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: The iso-to-allocortical representation of the multiple-demand gradient was preserved within thirds of the long-axis (correlation of r map with G3: 0.27 < r < 0.40).
source: While we found that the iso-to-allocortical representation of the multiple-demand gradient was preserved within thirds of the long-axis (correlation of r map with G3: 0.27 < r < 0.40)
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis within anterior-posterior segments.

claim: Long-axis position affected representation of macroscale topographies specifically with respect to the first, sensory-transmodal functional gradient (correlation of r map with G1: −0.41 < r < 0.45).
source: long-axis position nevertheless affected representation of macroscale topographies specifically with respect to the first, sensory-transmodal functional gradient (correlation of r map with G1: −0.41 < r < 0.45).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis within anterior-posterior segments.

claim: The anterior-posterior axis largely reflected connectivity transitions described by the sensory-transmodal functional gradient (r = −0.84, pspin <0.001).
source: Further elucidating preferential rs-fMRI connectivity patterns of the anterior-posterior axis, we indeed found that this largely reflected connectivity transitions described by the sensory-transmodal functional gradient (r = −0.84, pspin <0.001; Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis with spin permutation testing shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The transmodal anchor had stronger functional connectivity with the anterior aspect of the MTL, while the sensory anchor had stronger connectivity with the posterior aspect.
source: The transmodal anchor had stronger functional connectivity with the anterior aspect of the MTL, while the sensory anchor had stronger connectivity with the posterior aspect.
evidence: Supported by analysis of functional connectivity patterns.

claim: The association of anterior-posterior axis with the first functional gradient was specific, with higher correlation coefficients than the second (z = 19.21, p<0.001) and third (z = 30.23, p<0.001) gradients.
source: Again, the association was specific to one gradient, with higher correlation coefficients of the anterior-posterior axis with the first functional gradient than the second (z = 19.21, p<0.001) and third (z = 30.23, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: Functional findings from mesiotemporal confluence were virtually consistent when controlling for spatial SNR (rspatial = 0.92) and temporal SNR (rtemporal = 0.99) compared to the iso-to-allocortical axis.
source: While we indeed observed variations in both temporal as well as spatial SNR across the MTL, findings were virtually identical controlling for SNR via partial correlation [compared to the iso-to-allocortical axis from Figure 3B: rspatial = 0.92, rtemporal = 0.99
evidence: Supported by control analysis for signal-to-noise ratio effects.

claim: Functional findings from mesiotemporal confluence were virtually consistent when controlling for spatial SNR (rspatial = 0.99) and temporal SNR (rtemporal = 0.99) compared to the anterior-posterior axis.
source: compared to the anterior-posterior axis from Figure 3C: rspatial = 0.99, rtemporal = 0.99].
evidence: Supported by control analysis for signal-to-noise ratio effects.

claim: Functional findings from mesiotemporal confluence were virtually consistent when excluding temporal lobe regions as targets in the macrolevel functional connectivity findings (r = 0.85).
source: Similarly, functional findings from mesiotemporal confluence were virtually consistent when excluding of temporal lobe regions as targets in the macrolevel functional connectivity findings (compared to Figure 3F: r = 0.85).
evidence: Supported by control analysis excluding temporal lobe targets.

claim: In the replication dataset, decreasing effective connectivity was observed with increasing deviation from the iso-to-allocortical axis (riso = −0.24; rallo = −0.47).
source: In line with the original analysis, we observed decreasing effective connectivity with increasing deviation from the iso-to-allocortical axis (riso = −0.24; rallo = −0.47; Figure 4A)
evidence: Supported by replication analysis in HCP dataset shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the replication dataset, strength of isocortical rs-fMRI connectivity with the iso-to-allocortical axis corresponded with the multiple-demand functional gradient (r = −0.52, pspin <0.001).
source: As in the original analyses, strength of isocortical rs-fMRI connectivity with the iso-to-allocortical axis corresponded with the multiple-demand functional gradient (r = −0.52, pspin <0.001)
evidence: Supported by replication analysis in HCP dataset.

claim: In the replication dataset, variations in rs-fMRI connectivity along the anterior-posterior axis corresponded with the sensory-transmodal functional gradient (r = 0.33, pspin <0.001).
source: whereas variations in rs-fMRI connectivity along the anterior-posterior axis corresponded with the sensory-transmodal functional gradient (r = 0.33, pspin <0.001) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by replication analysis in HCP dataset shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The iso-to-allocortical axis is related to decreasing connectivity with multiple-demand systems.
source: The iso-to-allocortical axis is related to decreasing connectivity with multiple-demand systems - multimodal areas involved in external attention across multiple contexts (Fedorenko et al., 2013; Duncan, 2010)
evidence: Supported by functional connectivity analysis and citations to multiple-demand system research.

claim: The anterior-posterior axis reflected a shift from preference for transmodal cortex, such as the default-mode network, to sensory-and-motor regions.
source: while the anterior-posterior axis reflected a shift from preference for transmodal cortex, such as the default-mode network, to sensory-and-motor regions.
evidence: Supported by functional connectivity analysis.

claim: The anterior and posterior processing streams are successively integrated along steps of the iso-to-allocortical axis while external attentional processes are increasingly dampened.
source: Our results thus suggest that the anterior and posterior processing streams are successively integrated along steps of the iso-to-allocortical axis while external attentional processes are increasingly dampened.
evidence: Interpretation based on the functional connectivity findings.

claim: Higher-order representations constructed within the depths of the hippocampus flow from allo-to-isocortex before being broadcast back to sensory and transmodal areas.
source: Higher-order representations constructed within the depths of the hippocampus then flow from allo-to-isocortex before being broadcast back to sensory and transmodal areas.
evidence: Interpretation based on effective connectivity and functional connectivity findings.

claim: The 'hierarchy of associativity' is evidenced by invasive tract-tracing in non-human animals.
source: This 'hierarchy of associativity' is also evidenced by invasive tract-tracing in non-human animals (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to tract-tracing research.

claim: The MTL architecture could provide a neural workspace that is capable of representing both the abstract structure of tasks, as well as their specific sensory features.
source: and could provide a neural workspace that is capable of representing both the abstract structure of tasks, as well as their specific sensory features, thereby supporting the hypothesised role of the MTL in cognitive maps (O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978; Tolman, 1948; Behrens et al., 2018).
evidence: Interpretation based on findings and citations to cognitive map theory.

claim: The iso-to-allocortical axis mirrors a reduction in the diversity of projections.
source: The iso-to-allocortical axis also mirrors a reduction in the diversity of projections (Lavenex and Amaral, 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to anatomical research.

claim: Subfield-focused approaches have shown selective task activation along the iso-to-allocortical axis during pattern separation/completion.
source: These findings may help to understand the influence of cytoarchitecture and connectivity on functional dissociation within the MTL, as subfield-focused approaches have shown selective task activation along the iso-to-allocortical axis, for example during pattern separation/completion (Stevenson et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to task-based fMRI research.

claim: Subfield-focused approaches have shown selective task activation along the iso-to-allocortical axis during encoding/retrieval.
source: and encoding/retrieval (Suthana et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to task-based fMRI research.

claim: Sensory-transmodal differentiation of rs-fMRI connectivity along the MTL long axis is well-evidenced in the literature.
source: Sensory-transmodal differentiation of rs-fMRI connectivity along the MTL long axis is well-evidenced in the literature (Strange et al., 2014; Maass et al., 2015; Vos de Wael et al., 2018; Przeździk et al., 2019; Libby et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple rs-fMRI studies.

claim: Spatial gradients that reflect sensory-transmodal differentiation are evident in subcortical structures.
source: Spatial gradients that reflect sensory-transmodal differentiation are also evident in subcortical structures (Müller et al., 2020; Tian et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to subcortical gradient research.

claim: The cerebellum exhibits a functional gradient related to sensory-transmodal differentiation.
source: and the cerebellum (Guell et al., 2018).
evidence: Inferred from citation to cerebellar gradient research in context of sensory-transmodal differentiation.

claim: The cerebellum exhibits a second functional gradient related to multiple-demand processing.
source: Additionally, the cerebellum exhibits a second functional gradient related to multiple-demand processing (Guell et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to cerebellar gradient research.

claim: The repetition of gradients at various scales may relate to interconnectivity or result from shared participation in large-scale functional modes.
source: The repetition of gradients at various scales, from the whole cortex to within a brain region, may relate to interconnectivity or result from shared participation in large-scale functional modes.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of gradient findings.

claim: The left MTL exhibits nuanced cytoarchitectural differences to the right MTL.
source: In addition, this would allow replication in the left hemisphere, which exhibits nuanced cytoarchitectural differences to the right MTL (Zaidel, 1999; Barrera et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to research on hemispheric differences.

claim: The left and right MTL show asymmetry in task activations.
source: and asymmetry in task activations (Shipton et al., 2014; Miller et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to task-based fMRI research.

claim: Structural and functional perturbations of the MTL are at the core of Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy.
source: Given that structural and functional perturbations of the MTL are at the core of multiple brain diseases, notably Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, and drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy (Braak and Braak, 1991; Engel, 2001; Kim et al., 2015; Lisman et al., 2017; Bernhardt et al., 2016; Blümcke et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical research.

claim: Cytoarchitectural differentiation relates to patterns of intrinsic signal flow within the MTL microcircuit.
source: To conclude, our work shows that cytoarchitectural differentiation relates to patterns of intrinsic signal flow within the MTL microcircuit
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The long-axis allows for broad distribution of the computed neural code across the cortical hierarchy.
source: while the long-axis allows for broad distribution of the computed neural code across the cortical hierarchy.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Cytoarchitectural variation can partly account for both the convergence of distributed processing streams and distribution of integrated neural computations across large-scale systems.
source: By focusing on one of the most intriguing and integrative regions of the brain, this work illustrates how cytoarchitectural variation can partly account for both the convergence of distributed processing streams and distribution of integrated neural computations across large-scale systems.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The study provides clues for fundamental aspects of structure-function coupling in the brain.
source: More broadly, our study of the MTL may provide clues for fundamental aspects of structure-function coupling in the brain (Mesulam, 1998; Lavenex and Amaral, 2000)
evidence: Interpretation of study's broader implications with supporting citations.

claim: The study reveals core principles underlying macroscale cortical organisation.
source: and in revealing core principles underlying macroscale cortical organisation (Sanides, 1962; Dart, 1934; Abbie, 1938; Abbie, 1942; Goulas et al., 2019).
evidence: Interpretation of study's broader implications with supporting citations.

claim: The hippocampal model includes the subiculum and CA1-4.
source: The hippocampal model includes the subiculum and CA1-4.
evidence: Description of the anatomical model used in the study.

claim: The dentate gyrus was excluded from the hippocampal model because it is topologically disconnected in the unfolded space.
source: The dentate gyrus was excluded because it is topologically disconnected in the unfolded space (DeKraker et al., 2019).
evidence: Methodological decision explained with citation.

claim: The inner surface of the hippocampus, with respect to the hippocampal fissure, is continuous with the pial surface.
source: The inner surface of the hippocampus, with respect to the hippocampal fissure, is continuous with the pial surface, whereas the outer surface of the hippocampus is continuous with the white matter boundary (Amaral and Witter, 1989).
evidence: Anatomical description supported by citation.

claim: The outer surface of the hippocampus is continuous with the white matter boundary.
source: The inner surface of the hippocampus, with respect to the hippocampal fissure, is continuous with the pial surface, whereas the outer surface of the hippocampus is continuous with the white matter boundary (Amaral and Witter, 1989).
evidence: Anatomical description supported by citation.

claim: The study used 14 equivolumetric surfaces between the inner and outer confluent surfaces, resulting in 16 surfaces in total.
source: We generated 14 equivolumetric surfaces between the inner and outer confluent surfaces, resulting in 16 surfaces in total.
evidence: Description of the sampling methodology.

claim: Intensities were sampled from the 40 μm BigBrain blocks along 9432 matched vertices.
source: Then, we sampled the intensities from the 40 μm BigBrain blocks along 9432 matched vertices, creating microstructure profiles in the direction of cortical columns for the hippocampus and adjacent MTL areas.
evidence: Description of the sampling methodology.

claim: Merker staining is a form of silver impregnation for cell bodies that produces a high contrast of black pigment in cells on a virtually colourless background.
source: The Merker, 1983 staining is a form of silver impregnation for cell bodies that produces a high contrast of black pigment in cells on a virtually colourless background.
evidence: Description of the histological staining method.

claim: Stained histological sections were digitized at 20 µm.
source: Stained histological sections were then digitized at 20 µm, resulting in greyscale images with darker colouring where many or large cells occur.
evidence: Description of the digitization process.

claim: The study used an equivolumetric algorithm to optimise the fit of depth-wise surfaces with variations in thickness and curvature.
source: In lieu of precise laminar decomposition, which is currently untenable in such transition regions (Wagstyl et al., 2020), we utilised an equivolumetric algorithm to optimise the fit of depth-wise surfaces with variations in thickness and curvature (Waehnert et al., 2014).
evidence: Description of the surface sampling methodology with citations.

claim: Diffusion map embedding is optimally suited for multi-scale architectures because local geometries are preserved and then integrated into a set of global eigenvectors.
source: Diffusion map embedding is optimally suited for multi-scale architectures, because unlike global methods, such as principle component analysis and multidimensional scaling, local geometries are preserved and then integrated into a set of global eigenvectors.
evidence: Explanation of the methodological choice based on established knowledge.

claim: The study used resting state functional imaging data from 40 healthy adults (14 females, mean ± SD age = 30.4 ± 6.7, two left-handed).
source: We studied resting state functional imaging data from 40 healthy adults (microstructure informed connectomics (MICs) cohort; 14 females, mean ± SD age = 30.4 ± 6.7, two left-handed).
evidence: Description of the study sample.

claim: MRI data was acquired on a 3T Siemens Magnetom Prisma-Fit with a 64-channel head coil.
source: MRI data was acquired on a 3T Siemens Magnetom Prisma-Fit with a 64-channel head coil.
evidence: Description of the MRI acquisition hardware.

claim: The study used spectral dynamic causal modelling to estimate the effective connectivity between regions of the cortical confluence model.
source: Spectral dynamic causal modelling estimated the effective connectivity between regions of the cortical confluence model (Friston et al., 2014; Razi et al., 2015).
evidence: Description of the analysis method with citations.

claim: The study used a fourth order autoregressive model to estimate cross spectra of the timeseries.
source: In line with previous research (Friston et al., 2014; Razi et al., 2015), we used a fourth order autoregressive model to estimate cross spectra of the timeseries.
evidence: Description of the analysis method with citations.

claim: The study replicated fMRI findings in 40 unrelated healthy adults (14 females, age = 29.4 ± 3.8 years) from the Human Connectome Project.
source: We replicated the fMRI findings in 40 unrelated healthy adults (14 females, age = 29.4 ± 3.8 years) from the minimally preprocessed S900 release of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) (Glasser et al., 2013).
evidence: Description of the replication sample.

claim: The study was approved by the Research Ethics Board of the Montreal Neurological Institute and Hospital.
source: Participants whose data was studied in the main analysis provided informed consent, and the study was approved by the Research Ethics Board of the Montreal Neurological Institute and Hospital (2018–3469).
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: The dominant axis of MTL cytoarchitectural differentiation follows the iso-to-allocortical transition and depth-specific variations in neuronal density.
source: Leveraging an ultra-high-resolution histological reconstruction of a human brain, our study showed that the dominant axis of MTL cytoarchitectural differentiation follows the iso-to-allocortical transition and depth-specific variations in neuronal density.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract.

claim: The cytoarchitectural gradient was found to underpin intrinsic effective connectivity of the MTL, but patterns differed along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: Here, the cytoarchitectural gradient was found to underpin intrinsic effective connectivity of the MTL, but patterns differed along the anterior-posterior axis.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract.

claim: The iso-to-allocortical gradient parametrically represented the multiple-demand relative to task-negative networks.
source: Moreover, while the iso-to-allocortical gradient parametrically represented the multiple-demand relative to task-negative networks, anterior-posterior gradients represented transmodal versus unimodal networks.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract.

claim: Anterior-posterior gradients represented transmodal versus unimodal networks.
source: Moreover, while the iso-to-allocortical gradient parametrically represented the multiple-demand relative to task-negative networks, anterior-posterior gradients represented transmodal versus unimodal networks.
evidence: Summary of main finding from the abstract.

claim: The combination of micro- and macrostructural features allow the MTL to represent dominant motifs of whole-brain functional organisation.
source: Our findings establish that the combination of micro- and macrostructural features allow the MTL to represent dominant motifs of whole-brain functional organisation.
evidence: Summary conclusion from the abstract.
